title: The angels
hook: Jibril who brings revelation, Mika'il, Israfil, the recorders on each shoulder

segments.voice: Yesterday, nabi, the prophets, and your line: they are one family. How many names did you find? Today, the ones who carried the news to them. Day six hundred sixty-five, the end of a week.

Watch the end of a Muslim prayer. After the last sitting, the person praying turns their head to the right and says, peace be upon you and the mercy of Allah. Then to the left, the same words. If they're praying alone in an empty room, they still turn. Who are they greeting? Partly the people beside them, if there are any. And, many scholars say, someone who's always there: the angels. Today, the mala'ikah.

Mala'ikah is the plural; one angel is a malak. Many lexicons link it to a root for sending a message, and the Qur'an opens surah thirty-five by calling the angels messengers, with wings, two, three and four. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says they were created from light. Belief in them is one of the pillars of faith. A few are named. Jibril, Gabriel, brings the revelation down; the Qur'an names him in al-Baqarah, verse ninety-seven, as the one who brought it to the Prophet's heart. Mika'il, Michael, is named once, in the very next verse. Many Muslims know him from tradition as the angel connected with rain and provision. Israfil isn't named in the Qur'an at all. The Qur'an speaks of the trumpet that will be blown on the last Day, and the hadith tradition gives the angel of the trumpet the name Israfil. Then come the ones closest to daily life. Surah fifty says two receivers sit, one on the right and one on the left, and not a word is spoken without a watcher ready. Surah eighty-two calls them kiraman katibin: noble ones, writing, who know what you do. Many scholars teach that the one on the right records the good, and the one on the left the bad. And there's a hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim that says when someone intends a good deed and doesn't do it, it's still written as one good deed. Intending a bad one and holding back is written as a good deed too. The ones who write, it turns out, are generous with the pen.
screen: `ONE ON THE RIGHT, ONE ON THE LEFT.`

segments.voice: The practice: greet the angels on your right and left. Sit upright. Take a few slow breaths. Then turn your head gently to the right, and if you'd like, say the words of the prayer's end: as-salamu 'alaykum wa rahmatullah. Or simply let the greeting be silent. Turn back to center and breathe. Then turn to the left and do the same. Sit with the thought that whatever you said and did today was seen, and that a good intention counted, even the ones you didn't finish. The bell holds the time.
Mala'ikah. Angels, messengers of light: Jibril with revelation, Mika'il, Israfil with the trumpet, and the noble writers on the right and left. Today's word.

Your line: the ones who write. This week ran from once, nothing, through no thanks wanted, morning and evening, sent forth, don't deny it and they are one family. Today, give the writers on your right one good intention to record. Day six hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims count belief in angels among the pillars of faith; at the end of each prayer they turn the head to the right and then the left with the greeting of peace, which many scholars say includes the angels.

myth: Israfil is named in the Qur'an
the Qur'an mentions the trumpet; the name Israfil comes from the hadith tradition.
a good deed intended but not done is still written
a hadith in al-Bukhari and Muslim says it counts as one good deed.
the Qur'an describes angels with wings
surah thirty-five: wings, two, three and four.

fork.setup: you meant to call a sick friend today, and the day ran out. according to the hadith, what do the writers on your right record?
options: one good deed, for the intention.
fork.reveal: the hadith says a good intention not carried out is written as one good deed; carried out, it's multiplied.

trapdoor: what you thought: angels are winged figures in paintings.
what it means: mala'ikah are messengers made of light: Jibril, Mika'il, Israfil, and two noble writers beside each person.
what a scholar hears: Mika'il is named only in 2:98; Israfil's name comes from hadith, not the Qur'an; 50:17–18 places the recorders right and left.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 6491; Sahih Muslim 131 (good intentions recorded)
